t: What-If Scenario Engine - Signature build-tool concept
title: What-If Scenario Engine - Signature build-tool concept
definition: Compares outcomes under alternative assumptions.
description:
What-If Scenario Engine is the Signature build-tool concept that compares outcomes under alternative assumptions. In the Signature line, it is not a loose collection of scripts but a deterministic capability: the same build request produces the same verified result on every run, on every machine. This database documents the concept in full - what it is, the seven framework pillars that implement it, the real techniques it stands on, the standards it honors, and laddered drills that teach it from first principles to compounded mastery.

An AI that builds on demand needs What-If Scenario Engine the way a workshop needs its central bench. Without it, every build becomes improvisation: requirements drift, steps run out of order, and nobody can say why a result came out the way it did. With it, the build becomes a protocol - inputs declared, transformations explicit, outputs checked against the original request. That protocol is what these records describe, pillar by pillar.

Every record in this database carries a runnable demonstration program, because a build tool that cannot show its work cannot be trusted with real work. Read the overview, study the pillars, practice the drills, and run the demos: by the end the What-If Scenario Engine will be a capability you can invoke, not a concept you have read about.

t: Signature Programmer - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
title: Signature Programmer - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
definition: The Programmer component of the Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework, owning programmer. Signature concept.
description:
The Programmer is a load-bearing component of the Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework. Its contract is narrow and absolute: within the framework, everything concerning the framework's programmer responsibilities belongs to the Programmer, and the Programmer answers for it. This separation is what makes the framework testable - the Programmer can be exercised alone, with declared inputs and checkable outputs, long before it is wired into a full build.

In operation the Programmer works like this. A build request arrives carrying the What-If Scenario Engine charter (compares outcomes under alternative assumptions.). The Programmer reads its portion of the charter, performs its transformation, and hands a verified intermediate result to the next pillar. If its checks fail, it stops the line and reports exactly what was wrong, instead of passing corruption downstream. That fail-fast discipline is the Signature line's signature.

Signature-concept illustration: a builder asks for an small optimization job that needs What-If Scenario Engine. The Programmer takes the request's programmer responsibilities slice, applies the framework's deterministic procedure, and returns its result with a proof of what it did. Run this record's demo program to see the Programmer's core logic execute on a concrete example - the same logic, the same result, every run.

Signature framing: this pillar is part of the Signature line's original design for What-If Scenario Engine. It is labeled a Signature concept throughout - an engineered proposal, not an established public fact. The techniques it relies on are real and cited in the technique records of this database.

t: Signature Brancher - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
title: Signature Brancher - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
definition: The Brancher component of the Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework, owning brancher. Signature concept.
description:
Inside the Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework, the Brancher owns the framework's brancher responsibilities. Frameworks fail when responsibilities blur; the Signature line prevents that by giving each pillar a written contract, and the Brancher's contract is the sharpest of the seven. It accepts declared inputs, applies one deterministic transformation, and emits a result that any other pillar - or any auditor - can verify independently.

What distinguishes the Signature Brancher from an ad-hoc script is the verification loop. Every execution is checked against the charter (Compares outcomes under alternative assumptions.). If the result cannot be justified against the charter, it is rejected and the build halts with a diagnostic instead of a silent wrong answer. Deterministic builds are not a slogan here; they are the acceptance test.

Same seed, same output: that reproducibility is the entire point.

t: Signature Dispatcher - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
title: Signature Dispatcher - What-If Scenario Engine framework pillar
definition: The Dispatcher component of the Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework, owning dispatcher. Signature concept.
description:
The Signature What-If Scenario Engine framework decomposes the capability (Compares outcomes under alternative assumptions.) into seven pillars, and the Dispatcher is the one that owns the framework's dispatcher responsibilities. Owning a responsibility means three things in the Signature line: the pillar declares exactly what it accepts, it publishes exactly what it guarantees, and it logs enough evidence that a third party can replay its work and reach the same conclusion.

This discipline pays off when builds go wrong, because they always eventually do. When a What-If Scenario Engine result looks suspicious, the auditor does not re-run the whole build and hope; they replay the Dispatcher's log, check its guarantees against its inputs, and find the fault at its source. The pillar is thus both a worker and a witness - it does the work and it testifies about the work.

Try it yourself: this record's demo runs the Dispatcher's core procedure on a worked example. The program is plain JavaScript - save it as demo.js and run it with node, or press Run in the Demo Lab. Change the inputs and re-run; the procedure is deterministic, so you can verify every claim the description makes.

It is labeled a Signature concept throughout - an engineered proposal, not an established public fact. The techniques it relies on are real and cited in the technique records of this database.

Read the brief twice. List every input the What-If Scenario Engine needs, every output it must produce, and one contract each input-output pair must satisfy. Work it by hand first, then run the demo program and compare its trace against your own reasoning. When they agree, the concept is yours.
